extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers and policymakers interested in wartime policy, press censorship, and presidential security
extracted.subtask_description: A news-article–style treatment of wartime policy decisions and norms: reporting on President Roosevelt's secret nationwide tour, debates over wartime price controls and manpower mobilization, and questions about voluntary press censorship and presidential security. Extracts standards and procedural rules discussed or implemented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Man-power control proposal features
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal would allow the government to assign men — and possibly women — to specific jobs deemed essential to the war effort; mobilize fully and allocate available man power to industry, agriculture and the armed forces; prevent one industry from bidding for another’s skilled labor; forbid workers from leaving one job in a war industry for another without Government permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as the core elements of the man-power control plans under discussion by the Man-Power Commission and Congressional committees; some members urged a prior survey of all man-power requirements before sweeping measures, while proponents argued legislation was necessary to mobilize and allocate labor efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion of call under National Resources Mobilization Act
rubrics_metrics.description: Proclamation making 19-year-olds and other specified age groups liable for compulsory military service, enlarging groups previously called under the National Resources Mobilization Act of 1940.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as tapping about 107,000 in the 19-year-old class and extending the scope of calls; context: announced by War Services Minister J. T. Thompson and part of broader manpower mobilization measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential authority to stabilize prices, wages and salaries
rubrics_metrics.description: The measure directs the President to issue an order stabilizing wages, prices and salaries by Nov. 1 and, so far as practicable, to stabilize them at the levels of Sept. 15, 1942.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signed into law and explained as broad authority to control inflation; designed to hold levels to a recent benchmark date, with the President empowered to issue implementing orders and to intervene where necessary for the prosecution of the war effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wage and salary ceiling rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Wage and salary ceilings cannot be lower than the highest figures reached between Jan. 1 and Sept. 15, 1942.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The conference bill was adjusted so ceilings protect prior increases; the provision was modified so the President could act quickly where war demands or 'gross inequities' made it necessary, reflecting a balance between protecting past wage gains and enabling wartime controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Farm price ceiling and parity standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Farm price ceilings cannot be set below parity, or the highest market levels between Jan. 1 and Sept. 15, 1942, whichever is higher; if prices set fail to reflect increases in farm labor and other agricultural expenses since Jan. 1, 1941, they must be revised accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was worked out amid intense debate with farm interests seeking to include farm labor costs in parity formulas; the compromise sought to ensure farmers received a floor while allowing administrative adjustments to reflect cost changes since 1941.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crop loan rate rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Crop loan rate is fixed at 90 percent of parity for the duration of the war and for two years after hostilities end, with the President authorized to set the loan rate between 85 and 90 percent for corn and wheat if desirable to avoid high feed prices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained as a means to provide a floor below which farm prices may not drop, while allowing limited Presidential flexibility (85–90%) for certain staples to prevent undue rises in livestock and poultry feed costs; loans are based on parity price rather than market price.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public utility and common carrier rate procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Public utility and common carrier rates may be raised only on condition that such concerns give 30 days’ notice to the President and permit a representative of the price administrator to appear and intervene at state utility board hearings on behalf of the consumer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conference committee altered an original provision for broader Presidential authority into this procedural requirement, adding a consumer-protection element by allowing federal representation at state hearings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press censorship standard for presidential movements
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary wartime suppression of news about the President’s movements can be justified as a precaution for the Commander in Chief’s safety, but such censorship should not be carried to the point of keeping from the public events of obvious interest or becoming a precedent that undermines public confidence in the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial consensus described in the article: many papers voluntarily withheld the news to protect national security and the President, but commentators warned the self-imposed restraint risks public mistrust, could damage morale, and therefore should be used sparingly; proposals included making brief advance announcements of extended absences and limiting secrecy during political campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on secrecy when used during political campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: If movements must be covered by complete censorship, it raises a question about the propriety of presidential travel during political campaigns; secrecy of that sort may make such tours morally or politically questionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial views urged caution: if censorship is required, the President should refrain from nonessential tours in campaign periods; secrecy that breeds suspicion can damage public trust even when intended for safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational security measures for presidential travel
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational precautions to protect the President’s location include controlling identifiable clues (e.g., confining the presidential dog or removing its identification tag), limiting publication of itinerary details, and cooperating with voluntary press restraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the article: Secret Service instructed that the President’s dog be confined to the special train or have its tag removed; an entire union paper’s copies were destroyed after publishing the visit; the itinerary was kept secret until official release — all presented as concrete security practices used to shield movements.
